claims.text: The starting material is the HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of 786 MPa.
The starting alloy has a quasi-static compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The starting alloy has a quasi-static fracture strain of 13.5%.
Thermomechanical processing or controlled solidification can introduce nanoscale Nb- or V-rich precipitates into HfZrTiTa0.53.
Nb- or V-rich precipitates constitute a ductile phase in this alloy.
The nanoscale precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Precipitate impediment of dislocation motion promotes strain hardening.
The nanoscale precipitates delay strain localization.
The ductile nature of the precipitates enhances energy absorption and redistribution during deformation.
Enhanced energy absorption and redistribution mitigate rapid failure.
Enhanced energy absorption and redistribution reduce localized impact-induced energy release.
The precipitate-modified alloy will exhibit greater strain hardening than the baseline alloy under dynamic loading.
The precipitate-modified alloy will exhibit improved uniform deformation, represented by a fracture strain greater than 13.5%.
The precipitate-modified alloy will have greater resistance to strain localization than the baseline alloy.
The precipitate-modified alloy will exhibit reduced impact-induced energy release relative to the baseline.
The predicted effects apply at strain rates from 10^3 to 10^4 s^-1 under adiabatic high-speed-impact or shock-loading conditions.
The predicted effects may not apply under quasi-static or low-strain-rate loading.
The effectiveness of the precipitates depends on their size, distribution, and compatibility with the matrix.
